items.title: In 1952, A North Carolina Man Was The Best Man At His Friend’s Wedding. 10 Years Later, He Gave The Groom $125,000 To Invest. The Groom’s Name Was Warren Buffett. In 2014, Fred Stanback Donated $397 Million In Berkshire Stock To Charity.
items.summary: Fred Stanback was best man at Warren Buffett's wedding in 1952 and entrusted $125,000 to him in 1962. In 2014 he gave $397 million of Berkshire stock to charity without an announcement. Here is what the partnership letters and Berkshire's price say the $125,000 became, what that one gift would be worth today, and the four ways a 74-year-old retiree can give $30,000 from a stock that has grown tenfold, taxed four different ways.

items.title: Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.A) Turns To Yen Bonds As Japan Holdings Face Higher Rates
items.summary: Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE:BRK.A) issued more than ¥150b (over US$1b) in yen-denominated bonds to match its Japanese equity exposure. The new bonds carry maturities reportedly extending out to 30 years, aligning with the long holding period of Berkshire's investments in Japan. Management is using the yen funding to address currency and interest rate risk and to respond to wider TONA spreads in Japan. items.title: Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Just Hit a Record High as Nvidia Sank. A 67-Year-Old Who Bought 1,000 Shares in 2016 Can Sell $106,000 of It This Year and Pay 0% on the Gain
items.summary: Berkshire Hathaway rose all five days and closed Friday at a record $592.94, up 3.9% in the week Nvidia lost its CEO and fell 12.7%. A 67-year-old who bought 1,000 Class B shares ten years ago at $157.93 holds $592,940 and a $435,010 gain in a stock that pays no dividend. Under 2026's 0% capital gains ceiling he can sell 179 shares, about $106,000, and owe nothing on the gain; the only cost is $2,075 of tax on Social Security that the sale makes taxable.
